comments:
The problem seems to be that your `i18nFile` has the `.xliff` extension, not `.xlf`. Since the extension seems to be the primary way to identify a suitable translation parser, this causes a mismatch when searching for a parser.

I don't know what the expected behavior should be here. @clydin Could you suggest what needs to be done, if anything?

The translation file parsers contained within the `@angular/localize` package control the detection of the file format.  For xliff1 files the relevant code can be found [here](https://github.com/angular/angular/blob/939e2f76f6c3180e13886357a7dbdf8d562e98f4/packages/localize/src/tools/src/translate/translation_files/translation_parsers/xliff1_translation_parser.ts#L31).  Currently, the code to determine the format checks for the `xlf` extension and not the `xliff` extension.  This code could potentially be expanded.  @petebacondarwin may have more insight into this though.

Had a similar issue (working fine without Ivy, "Unsupported translation file format" in Ivy): for me the file extension was fine (`.xlf`) but our translation system did not set an XML Namespace (`xmlns`) on the XLIFF localized dictionaries, causing the second condition (`XLIFF_1_2_NS_REGEX.test(contents)`) in the code pointed by @clydin to return `false`.

Actually looking at the [XLIFF 1.2 standard](http://docs.oasis-open.org/xliff/v1.2/os/xliff-core.html):

> If necessary, you can also specify a namespace for XLIFF. The namespace identifier for this standard is "urn:oasis:names:tc:xliff:document:1.2".
>
>A minimal XLIFF document with one entry looks something like this:
>```
><?xml version="1.0"?>
><xliff version="1.2">
><file source-language="EN" datatype="plaintext" original="file.ext">
><body>
><trans-unit id="1">
><source>Hello World!</source>
></trans-unit>
></body>
></file>
>```

i.e., it looks like `@angular/localize` is a bit too strict when it comes to matching XLIFF 1.2 files.

For sure we can relax the file extension check. The problem after that is how to tell XLIFF 1.2 files from XLIFF 2.0 file? I guess we should be just checking the `version` attribute on the `xliff` element.

Moreover we could even ditch the file-extension check altogether and just look for an XML file that has the `<xliff version='XXX'>` element? WDYT?

> Moreover we could even ditch the file-extension check altogether and just look for an XML file that has the <xliff version='XXX'> element? WDYT?

Given that the goal here is only to tell apart XLIFF 1.2 files from XLIFF 2.0, XMB, or JSON ones, IMO just looking at the `<xliff version="XXX">` does the job.
Closing as #35793 has been merged and is available in 9.0.6
@nodermatt I don't know, sorry. The extension doesn't seem to be relevant anymore, maybe there's something wrong in the XML contents.

```

And see if you get a more detailed error message...
